sources.name: SPARQL 1.1 Query Language
sources.role: RDF graph-pattern matching, query form, solution sequence, expression, aggregation and dataset-selection contract
verified_facts: SPARQL 1.1 defines a query language for RDF and evaluates graph patterns against an RDF dataset.
Query forms include SELECT, CONSTRUCT, ASK and DESCRIBE, with solution modifiers such as ordering, projection and limits.
Query evaluation can depend on the active graph, named graphs, dataset clauses and the entailment regime exposed by the service.
semantic_limits: A syntactically valid query and successful result prove evaluation against the selected dataset state, not source authority, completeness or physical truth.
CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE results are derived RDF graphs and must not be treated as exact downloaded source bytes or immutable object identity.
ASK=true or a returned numeric literal must not create a parcel-height row without authoritative source bytes, exact polygon, CRS, vertical datum, units, method and execution receipts.

sources.name: RDF 1.1 Concepts and Abstract Syntax
sources.role: RDF triple, graph, dataset, IRI, literal, blank-node, graph-isomorphism and source-snapshot contract
verified_facts: RDF graphs are sets of subject-predicate-object triples whose terms are IRIs, literals or blank nodes.
An RDF dataset contains one default graph and zero or more named graphs.
Blank-node identifiers are local to a serialization or store, and RDF sources may expose different graph snapshots over time.
semantic_limits: An RDF statement is a claim in a graph; the data model does not independently verify that the claim matches the physical world.
Graph isomorphism or term equality does not establish equality of original source bytes, download completeness or scientific accuracy.
Blank-node labels and graph names must not be reused as persistent cadastral parcel identity or measurement provenance.

sources.name: RDF 1.1 Turtle
sources.role: compact RDF textual syntax, prefixes, base IRI, literals, blank nodes, collections, grammar and parser contract
verified_facts: Turtle is a concrete textual syntax capable of expressing an RDF graph in compact form.
Turtle provides prefix and base declarations, RDF literals, blank nodes, collections and a normative grammar.
Turtle conformance applies to documents and parsers that convert the concrete syntax into RDF triples.
semantic_limits: Successful Turtle parsing establishes syntax-to-graph conversion, not authority, truth, completeness or numeric accuracy.
Base-IRI resolution and prefix expansion affect the produced RDF terms and therefore must be pinned when evidence is compared.
Different Turtle byte streams can express the same RDF graph, so graph equality cannot replace exact-object digest and source-byte receipts.

sources.name: RDF 1.1 Semantics
sources.role: RDF interpretation, truth condition, entailment, equivalence, inconsistency and inference-rule contract
verified_facts: RDF 1.1 Semantics defines model-theoretic interpretations and truth conditions for RDF graphs.
Entailment holds when every interpretation satisfying one graph also satisfies the entailed graph under the selected regime.
Semantic inconsistency means no interpretation satisfies the graph under the applicable conditions.
semantic_limits: Entailment is conditional on the asserted premises and semantic regime; it does not independently establish that those premises are factual or authoritative.
Logical consistency proves only the absence of contradiction under the model and is not evidence of source completeness or measurement accuracy.
An entailed numeric statement must not become a terrain result without exact source object, cadastral geometry, CRS, vertical datum, units, algorithm and execution receipts.
